evidence.supportingExcerpt: In RESPONDER, 398 women with stage I to III breast cancer of all biological subtypes and an imaging response were analysed. Vacuum-assisted biopsy missed residual cancer in 37 of the 208 women whose surgery found it: a false-negative rate of 17.8% (95% confidence interval 12.8% to 23.7%). Of the 37 misses, 20 had minimal residual tumour smaller than 5 mm. Exploratory analyses reported no false negatives with the largest-volume 7-gauge needle and a 6.2% false-negative rate (95% confidence interval 3.4% to 10.5%) when imaging and biopsy were combined. These refinements do not establish general omission safety.

proofs.requirement: The original-only Kuerer cohort is a single-arm phase 2 selection of 50 women aged at least 40 with TNBC or HER2-positive cancer, residual lesion under 2 cm and at least 12 cores; those conditions constrain interpretation.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: The 2025 single-arm omission study enrolled 50 women aged at least 40 with HER2-positive or triple-negative cT1-2N0-1M0 disease and an imaging residual lesion smaller than 2 cm. After at least twelve 9-gauge vacuum cores, 31 had no residual breast cancer on biopsy and received radiotherapy without breast surgery. No ipsilateral breast recurrences occurred at median follow-up 55.4 months. Patients initially node-positive still underwent targeted axillary dissection. This small uncontrolled study calls for confirmation.

For these biopsy studies, breast pCR definitions can require no invasive or in-situ disease, while other breast pCR endpoints allow residual in-situ disease and include nodal status. They are not independent replications.

proofs.requirement: A biopsy-defined response samples the bed. Trial design, selection, imaging and reference surgery or follow-up limit generalization; the lesson route to comparison trials does not itself establish a current surgical policy.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Image-guided biopsy after preoperative systemic treatment tests selected parts of the former breast tumour bed. Diagnostic accuracy studies compare it with subsequent surgery; an omission study instead follows selected people without breast surgery. These designs answer different questions.

A small single-arm cohort with zero recurrences leaves uncertainty without a randomised comparison. Sampling does not provide the oriented margins or complete residual-burden assessment of resection, and breast biopsy does not assess every axillary node. Missing residual disease can also miss information used for further treatment decisions. These studies support continued investigation rather than a general rule to omit surgery.
